# Classy Store

Class-based reactive state management for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Angular. Write plain TypeScript classes — get fine-grained reactivity, immutable snapshots, and zero-boilerplate hooks.

```
ES6 Proxy · useSyncExternalStore · proxy-compare
```

## Features

- **Class-based stores** — plain classes with fields, methods, and getters
- **No wrappers** — no `observer()`, no `Provider`, no HOCs, no decorators
- **Fine-grained reactivity** — components only re-render when properties they read change
- **Immutable snapshots** — structural sharing keeps unchanged sub-trees reference-equal
- **Memoized computed values** — class getters are automatically cached, recompute only when deps change
- **Batched subscriptions** — ordinary listeners coalesce mutations in a microtask; React receives updates synchronously
- **Type-safe** — full TypeScript inference from your class definitions
- **Framework bindings** — first-class integrations for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Angular
- **Two hook modes** — explicit selector or automatic property tracking (React)
- **Reactive collections** — `reactiveMap()` and `reactiveSet()` for Map/Set-like state
- **Persistence** — `persist()` utility with transforms, versioning, migration, debounce, cross-tab sync, TTL expiration, and SSR support
- **DevTools** — `devtools()` connects to Redux DevTools for state inspection and time-travel debugging
- **Property subscriptions** — `subscribeKey()` watches a single property for changes with previous/current values
- **Undo/Redo** — `withHistory()` adds undo/redo via a snapshot stack with pause/resume and configurable limits

## Installation

Upgrading from 0.7.x? Read the [0.8.0 upgrade guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/UPGRADING_0_8) for public API changes and persistence error handling. From 0.6.x or earlier, also follow the [0.7.0 upgrade guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/UPGRADING_0_7).

```bash
bun add @codebelt/classy-store
```

All framework peer dependencies are optional — install only what your project uses:

| Framework | Peer Dependency | Import |
|-----------|----------------|--------|
| React | `react >= 18.0.0` | `@codebelt/classy-store/react` |
| Vue | `vue >= 3.0.0` | `@codebelt/classy-store/vue` |
| Svelte | `svelte >= 4.0.0` | `@codebelt/classy-store/svelte` |
| Solid | `solid-js >= 1.0.0` | `@codebelt/classy-store/solid` |
| Angular | `@angular/core >= 17.0.0` | `@codebelt/classy-store/angular` |

## Quick Start

### 1. Define a store class

```typescript
class TodoStore {
  todos: Todo[] = [];
  filter: 'all' | 'done' | 'pending' = 'all';

  // Getter = computed value
  get filtered() {
    if (this.filter === 'all') return this.todos;
    return this.todos.filter((todo) =>
        this.filter === 'done' ? todo.done : !todo.done,
    );
  }

  get remaining() {
    return this.todos.filter((todo) => !todo.done).length;
  }

  addTodo(text: string) {
    this.todos.push({text, done: false});
  }

  toggle(index: number) {
    this.todos[index]!.done = !this.todos[index]!.done;
  }
}
```

### 2. Create a reactive store

```typescript
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

const todoStore = createClassyStore(new TodoStore());
```

### 3. Use in React components

```tsx
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

// Selector mode: explicit control over what triggers re-renders
function TodoCount() {
  const remaining = useClassyStore(todoStore, (state) => state.remaining);
  return <span>{remaining} left</span>;
}

// Auto-tracked mode: reads are tracked automatically
function TodoList() {
  const snap = useClassyStore(todoStore);
  return (
    <ul>
      {snap.filtered.map((todo, index) => (
        <li key={index}>{todo.text}</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}

// Actions: call methods directly on the store
function AddButton() {
  return <button onClick={() => todoStore.addTodo('New')}>Add</button>;
}
```

## Choosing an API

| What you need | API |
| --- | --- |
| Create shared state from a class or object | `createClassyStore(instance)` |
| Render store data in React | `useClassyStore(store)` or `useClassyStore(store, selector)` |
| Create a store owned by a component | `useLocalStore(factory)` |
| Bind a reusable hook to an existing store | `createStoreHook(store)` |
| Render undo/redo availability or pause state | `useHistoryStatus(history)` |
| Render persistence hydration, expiry, or errors | `usePersistStatus(handle)` |
| Prepare matching initial data for SSR/hydration | `prepareStoreForHydration(store)` |
| Read state outside React or observe mutations | `snapshot(store)`, `subscribe(store, listener)`, `subscribeKey(store, key, listener)` |
| Persist state, record history, or inspect it in DevTools | `persist(store, options)`, `withHistory(store)`, `devtools(store)` |
| Track changes inside Map-like or Set-like collections | `reactiveMap()`, `reactiveSet()` |
| Compare selector results one level deep | `shallowEqual(previous, next)` |

`useClassyStore` is the starting point for React components. The two status hooks
are optional: use them only when displaying metadata from an existing history or
persistence handle. They do not create those handles or subscribe to store data.

## Package entry points

Import from the entry that owns the API. Core, collections, and utilities do not depend on React.

| Import path | Runtime exports | Public types |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `@codebelt/classy-store` | `createClassyStore`, `snapshot`, `subscribe`, `shallowEqual` | `Snapshot`, `SubscribeOptions` |
| `@codebelt/classy-store/react` | `useClassyStore`, `useLocalStore`, `createStoreHook`, `useHistoryStatus`, `usePersistStatus` | `UseClassyStoreSelectorOptions` |
| `@codebelt/classy-store/react/server` | `prepareStoreForHydration` | — |
| `@codebelt/classy-store/collections` | `reactiveMap`, `reactiveSet` | `ReactiveMap`, `ReactiveSet` |
| `@codebelt/classy-store/utils` | `persist`, `withHistory`, `subscribeKey`, `devtools` | `PersistOptions`, `PersistHandle`, `PersistStatus`, `PersistOperation`, `PropertyTransform`, `StorageAdapter`, `HistoryOptions`, `HistoryHandle`, `HistoryStatus`, `DevtoolsOptions`, `SubscribeOptions` |

`ReactiveMap` and `ReactiveSet` are exported as types; construct values with the
factory functions. The React entry carries `use client`. Import hydration
preparation from `/react/server` in both server code and client modules.

## API Reference

### `createClassyStore(instance)`

Wraps a class instance in a reactive Proxy. Mutations notify React immediately; ordinary subscribers are batched via `queueMicrotask`.

```typescript
const myStore = createClassyStore(new MyClass());
```

- **Methods** are automatically bound so `this` mutations go through the proxy
- **Getters** are automatically memoized — they only recompute when a dependency changes (like MobX `@computed`)
- **Nested objects/arrays** are lazily deep-proxied on first access

### `useClassyStore(store, selector?, options?)`

React hook that subscribes to store changes via `useSyncExternalStore`.

```typescript
type UseClassyStoreSelectorOptions<S> = {
  isEqual?: (previous: S, next: S) => boolean;
};
```

**Selector mode:**

```typescript
const count = useClassyStore(myStore, (state) => state.count);
const user = useClassyStore(myStore, (state) => state.user);
const items = useClassyStore(myStore, (state) => state.items);
```

The selector receives an immutable snapshot. Re-renders only when the selected value changes via `Object.is` by default, or `options.isEqual`.

**Auto-tracked mode:**

```typescript
const snap = useClassyStore(myStore);
// Access snap.count, snap.user.name, etc.
// Only re-renders when accessed properties change
```

Returns a tracking proxy. Properties your component reads are automatically tracked. Committed reads remain associated with each reused immutable snapshot object, so memoized calculations and children stay reactive even when they skip property reads on a later render. Abandoned renders do not publish their reads. Unchanged snapshots and nested tracked values retain their references across parent re-renders.

Auto-tracking requires native `WeakRef` support (ES2021). Tracking dependencies use weak references so cached child proxies do not keep obsolete collection snapshots alive. Applications still own references they explicitly retain, and stores prepared for hydration deliberately retain their initial snapshot while that store remains reachable.

**Custom equality:**

```typescript
import {shallowEqual} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

const userData = useClassyStore(myStore, (state) => ({
  name: state.user.name,
  role: state.user.role,
}), {isEqual: shallowEqual});
```

**Controlled input timing:**

```tsx
const name = useClassyStore(formStore, (state) => state.name);

return (
  <input
    value={name}
    onChange={(event) => formStore.setName(event.target.value)}
  />
);
```

React subscriptions always notify synchronously, including selector, auto-tracked, and bound hooks. There is no React `sync` option. This lets React observe controlled-field changes during the input event and preserve caret position. Ordinary `subscribe()` callbacks remain batched.

Migration: remove `{sync: true}` or `{sync: false}` from React hook calls and remove imports of `UseClassyStoreOptions`. Selector options still support `isEqual`. Synchronous notification does not make a method transactional: selectors can observe each write, while React batches rendering within event handlers.

### `useHistoryStatus(history)`

Use `useClassyStore(store)` for application data. Use `useHistoryStatus(history)` when a component renders undo/redo availability, recording state, or history disposal:

```tsx
import {useHistoryStatus} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import type {HistoryHandle} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

function UndoButton({history}: {history: HistoryHandle}) {
  const {canUndo} = useHistoryStatus(history);
  return <button disabled={!canUndo} onClick={history.undo}>Undo</button>;
}
```

The hook accepts the `HistoryHandle` returned by `withHistory(store)` and returns `HistoryStatus`: `canUndo`, `canRedo`, `isPaused`, and `isDisposed`. It updates even when store data stays unchanged, such as when recording is paused. Creating or using history does not require the hook.

### `usePersistStatus(handle)`

Use `usePersistStatus(handle)` when a component renders persistence hydration, expiry, disposal, or errors:

```tsx
import {usePersistStatus} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import type {PersistHandle} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

function PersistenceBadge({handle}: {handle: PersistHandle}) {
  const {isHydrated, lastError} = usePersistStatus(handle);
  if (lastError) return <span>Persistence failed: {lastError.operation}</span>;
  return <span>{isHydrated ? 'Ready' : 'Restoring…'}</span>;
}
```

The hook accepts the `PersistHandle` returned by `persist(store, options)` and returns `PersistStatus`: `isHydrated`, `isExpired`, `isDisposed`, and `lastError` (`{error, operation}` or `null`). `isHydrated` means a hydration attempt settled; inspect `lastError` for a reported failure. Configuring persistence and calling its methods do not require the hook.

Both hooks return readonly status snapshots whose identity stays stable until a status field changes. They share an internal subscription implementation. Status listeners run synchronously when status changes; ordinary store subscriptions, including history recording, remain batched. Unmounting a status consumer removes its listener without disposing the handle.

Outside React, both handles provide framework-neutral status methods: `getSnapshot()`, `getServerSnapshot()`, and `subscribe(listener)`, which returns listener cleanup.

For SSR, handles expose their initial status through `getServerSnapshot()` and React catches up with live status after hydration. Construct request-scoped handles and matching client handles with the same initial status; keep persistence side effects in the provider lifecycle described in [React store scoping](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SCOPING).

### `prepareStoreForHydration(store)`

Captures the initial snapshot for server rendering and client hydration, returning the same mutable store proxy:

```ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {prepareStoreForHydration} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react/server';

const store = prepareStoreForHydration(
  createClassyStore(new ProfileStore(initialData)),
);
```

Call on each request's store and its client counterpart using matching initial data, before rendering or starting persistence. Direct and bound hooks hydrate from the captured snapshot even if persistence updates the live store before a Suspense boundary hydrates. After hydration they read current state normally.

Preparation is idempotent, retains the first snapshot for the store's lifetime, and applies to the exact proxy passed in. Client-only apps need no preparation. See [React SSR and hydration](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SSR) for streaming, request isolation, nested proxies, and snapshot leaf semantics.

Import the preparation helper from `@codebelt/classy-store/react/server` on both the server and client. It does not import React hooks; the separate `/react` hooks entry is marked `use client`. See [Next.js App Router](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_NEXT) for production package boundaries and navigation patterns.

### `useLocalStore(factory)`

Creates a component-scoped reactive store. Each component instance gets its own isolated store. Unmounting releases React's reference; the store can be garbage collected when no other references remain.

```tsx
import {useLocalStore, useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

class CounterStore {
  count = 0;
  increment() { this.count++; }
}

function Counter() {
  const store = useLocalStore(() => new CounterStore());
  const count = useClassyStore(store, (state) => state.count);

  return <button onClick={() => store.increment()}>Count: {count}</button>;
}
```

Subsequent re-renders reuse the same store instance. Keep the factory pure: React StrictMode can invoke the initializer more than once in development.

For a shared subtree, use the [typed context and lifecycle example](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SCOPING). It covers independent and nested instances, explicit resets with React keys, effect cleanup, persistence, and SSR. `useLocalStore` owns the instance reference; application side effects still need cleanup in their effects.

> See the [Local Stores](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/TUTORIAL#local-stores) section in the Tutorial for persistence patterns and more examples.

### `createStoreHook(store)`

Creates a pre-bound React hook for a specific store proxy. Eliminates the boilerplate of writing a typed wrapper around `useClassyStore` for every store instance.

```tsx
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {createStoreHook} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

class CatalogPageStore {
  items: string[] = [];
  loading = false;

  get count() { return this.items.length; }

  addItem(item: string) { this.items.push(item); }
}

const catalogStore = createClassyStore(new CatalogPageStore());
export const useCatalogStore = createStoreHook(catalogStore);
```

The returned hook supports both selector mode and auto-tracked mode — identical to `useClassyStore`, but with the store already bound:

```tsx
// Selector mode
function ItemCount() {
  const count = useCatalogStore((state) => state.count);
  return <span>{count} items</span>;
}

// Auto-tracked mode
function ItemList() {
  const snap = useCatalogStore();
  return <ul>{snap.items.map((item) => <li key={item}>{item}</li>)}</ul>;
}

// Custom equality
import {shallowEqual} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

function Summary() {
  const data = useCatalogStore(
    (state) => ({count: state.count, loading: state.loading}),
    {isEqual: shallowEqual},
  );
  return <div>{data.loading ? 'Loading...' : `${data.count} items`}</div>;
}
```

Validates at creation time — throws if the argument is not a store proxy.

### `snapshot(store)`

Reads a snapshot with frozen copies of store objects and arrays, cached by store version with structural sharing. Used internally by `useClassyStore` but also available directly. Opaque leaves such as native `Map`, `Set`, `Date`, and functions retain their references; do not mutate them through a snapshot.

```typescript
import {snapshot} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

const snap = snapshot(myStore);
// Copied objects and arrays are frozen; mutate the store, not its snapshot.
// Structural sharing: unchanged sub-trees === previous snapshot
```

### `subscribe(store, callback, options?)`

Low-level subscription API. Returns an unsubscribe function. By default, the callback fires once per batched mutation after the microtask flush. Pass `{sync: true}` to notify immediately on each mutation.

```typescript
import {subscribe} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

const unsub = subscribe(myStore, () => {
  console.log('Store changed');
});

const unsubSync = subscribe(
  myStore,
  () => {
    console.log('Store changed synchronously');
  },
  {sync: true},
);

// Later: unsub();
```

### `shallowEqual(a, b)`

Shallow equality comparison for objects and arrays. Useful as a custom `isEqual` for selectors that return derived objects.

### `reactiveMap<K, V>(initial?)`

Creates a reactive Map-like collection backed by a plain array. Use inside a `createClassyStore()` for full reactivity. Import from `@codebelt/classy-store/collections`.

```typescript
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {reactiveMap} from '@codebelt/classy-store/collections';
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

class UserStore {
  users = reactiveMap<string, { name: string; role: string }>();

  addUser(id: string, name: string, role: string) {
    this.users.set(id, {name, role});
  }

  removeUser(id: string) {
    this.users.delete(id);
  }
}

const userStore = createClassyStore(new UserStore());

function UserList() {
  const snap = useClassyStore(userStore, (state) => [...state.users.entries()]);
  return (
    <ul>
      {snap.map(([id, user]) => (
        <li key={id}>{user.name} ({user.role})</li>
      ))}
    </ul>
  );
}
```

Supports: `.get()`, `.set()`, `.has()`, `.delete()`, `.clear()`, `.size`, `.keys()`, `.values()`, `.entries()`, `.forEach()`, `for...of`.

### `reactiveSet<T>(initial?)`

Creates a reactive Set-like collection backed by a plain array. Use inside a `createClassyStore()` for full reactivity. Import from `@codebelt/classy-store/collections`.

```typescript
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {reactiveSet} from '@codebelt/classy-store/collections';
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

class TagStore {
  tags = reactiveSet<string>();

  addTag(tag: string) {
    this.tags.add(tag);
  }
}

const tagStore = createClassyStore(new TagStore());

function TagList() {
  const tags = useClassyStore(tagStore, (state) => [...state.tags]);
  return tags.map(tag => <span key={tag}>{tag}</span>);
}
```

Supports: `.add()`, `.has()`, `.delete()`, `.clear()`, `.size`, `.keys()`, `.values()`, `.entries()`, `.forEach()`, `for...of`.

> **Note:** `reactiveMap()` and `reactiveSet()` are not real `Map`/`Set` instances — they emulate the API on top of plain arrays so the store proxy can track mutations. `instanceof Map` / `instanceof Set` will return `false`.

### `Snapshot<T>`

TypeScript utility type that converts a store type to its deeply readonly snapshot equivalent.

```typescript
import type {Snapshot} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

type MyStoreSnap = Snapshot<MyStore>;
// All properties are readonly, arrays become ReadonlyArray, etc.
```

## Collections (`@codebelt/classy-store/collections`)

Reactive Map and Set types are available via a separate entry point:

```typescript
import {reactiveMap, reactiveSet} from '@codebelt/classy-store/collections';
```

## Utilities (`@codebelt/classy-store/utils`)

Tree-shakeable utilities are available via a separate entry point:

```typescript
import {persist, devtools, subscribeKey, withHistory} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';
```

### `persist(store, options)`

Persist store state to storage with transforms, versioning, migration, cross-tab sync, and SSR support. Getters and methods are automatically excluded.

```typescript
import {persist} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

const handle = persist(todoStore, {name: 'todo-store', storage: localStorage});

// When this store's owner no longer needs persistence:
handle.dispose();
```

> See the [Persist Tutorial](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/PERSIST_TUTORIAL) and [Persist Architecture](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/PERSIST_ARCHITECTURE).

### `devtools(store, options?)`

Connect a store to Redux DevTools for state inspection and time-travel debugging.

```typescript
import {devtools} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

const disconnect = devtools(myStore, {name: 'MyStore'});
```

> See the [DevTools Tutorial](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/DEVTOOLS_TUTORIAL).

### `subscribeKey(store, key, callback, options?)`

Subscribe to changes on a single property, comparing snapshot values with `Object.is`. Notifications are batched by default; pass `{sync: true}` as the fourth argument to observe each change immediately. Returns listener cleanup.

```typescript
import {subscribeKey} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

const unsub = subscribeKey(store, 'theme', (value, prev) => {
  console.log(`Theme: ${prev} → ${value}`);
});
```

> See the [subscribeKey Tutorial](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/SUBSCRIBE_KEY_TUTORIAL).

### `withHistory(store, options?)`

Add undo/redo capability via a snapshot stack with pause/resume and configurable limits.

```typescript
import {withHistory} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

const history = withHistory(store, {limit: 100});
history.undo();
history.redo();
```

> See the [withHistory Tutorial](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/HISTORY_TUTORIAL).

## Patterns

### Multiple stores

```typescript
const authStore = createClassyStore(new AuthStore());
const uiStore = createClassyStore(new UiStore());

function Header() {
  const user = useClassyStore(authStore, (state) => state.currentUser);
  const theme = useClassyStore(uiStore, (state) => state.theme);
  return <header className={theme}>{user?.name}</header>;
}
```

### Class inheritance

Subclasses work out of the box. Methods, getters, and `super` calls from any ancestor are fully reactive:

```typescript
class BaseStore {
  loading = false;
  error: string | null = null;

  get hasError() { return this.error !== null; }
  setLoading(value: boolean) { this.loading = value; }
  setError(msg: string | null) { this.error = msg; }
}

class UserStore extends BaseStore {
  users: string[] = [];

  get count() { return this.users.length; }

  addUser(name: string) {
    this.users.push(name);
  }
}

const userStore = createClassyStore(new UserStore());

// Base methods, derived methods, base getters, derived getters — all reactive.
// snapshot(userStore) instanceof UserStore === true
```

### Nested object mutations

Nested objects are deeply reactive. Mutations at any depth trigger the correct re-renders:

```typescript
class SettingsStore {
  settings = {
    theme: 'dark',
    notifications: {
      email: true,
      push: false,
    },
  };

  togglePush() {
    this.settings.notifications.push = !this.settings.notifications.push;
  }
}

const settingsStore = createClassyStore(new SettingsStore());

// Only re-renders when push notification setting changes
function PushToggle() {
  const push = useClassyStore(settingsStore, (state) => state.settings.notifications.push);
  return <Switch checked={push} onChange={() => settingsStore.togglePush()} />;
}
```

### Array operations

Arrays support all standard operations — `push`, `splice`, `pop`, `shift`, index assignment, etc. Ordinary subscribers receive one microtask notification for consecutive mutations:

```typescript
class ListStore {
  items: string[] = [];

  addMany(newItems: string[]) {
    // Multiple pushes = one ordinary subscription notification
    for (const item of newItems) {
      this.items.push(item);
    }
  }

  removeAt(index: number) {
    this.items.splice(index, 1);
  }
}
```

### Computed getters (automatic memoization)

Class getters are automatically memoized at two levels — no `computed()` wrapper needed:

**Write proxy:** getters track which properties they read. The result is cached and only recomputes when a dependency changes:

```typescript
class Store {
  items = ['a', 'b', 'c'];
  filter = 'all';

  get filtered() {
    // Only runs when `items` or `filter` changes.
    // Accessing store.filtered multiple times returns the same reference.
    if (this.filter === 'all') return this.items;
    return this.items.filter(item => item === this.filter);
  }

  get filteredCount() {
    // Nested getters work: reads this.filtered (itself memoized)
    return this.filtered.length;
  }
}
```

**Snapshots:** getter results are stable across snapshots when dependencies haven't changed. This means selectors that return computed values work with `Object.is` by default — no `shallowEqual` needed:

```typescript
// Stable reference across re-renders when items/filter haven't changed.
// No shallowEqual required!
const filtered = useClassyStore(myStore, (state) => state.filtered);
```

### Working with Date and RegExp

`Date` and `RegExp` are **not proxied** — they are treated as opaque values. Replace them entirely to trigger an update:

```typescript
class Store {
  date = new Date();
  regex = /test/;

  updateDate() {
    // ❌ Mutation: won't trigger update
    // this.date.setFullYear(2025);

    // ✅ Replacement: triggers update
    this.date = new Date();
  }
}
```

For `Map` and `Set` semantics, use [`reactiveMap()`](#reactivemapk-vinitial) and [`reactiveSet()`](#reactivesettinitial) instead of native `Map`/`Set`.

## React Compiler compatibility

Direct and bound hooks work in compiled consumers with either selectors or auto-tracking. The regression matrix compiles consumer components with React Compiler 1.0 using default inference, then runs them against the packed library on React 18.0, 18.3, and 19.3. Fixtures must report successful compilation with memo slots; silently skipped components fail the checks. The library does not require a `"use no memo"` directive or custom compiler configuration.

Auto-tracking retains earlier committed reads while an immutable snapshot object is reused, including structurally shared children. This protects dependencies inside cached helpers, array calculations, and memoized children. After a conditional branch changes, an earlier read can still trigger an extra render until that snapshot object's identity changes. Use an explicit selector when exact selected-value equality matters.

Read render data through `useClassyStore` or a bound hook. The original store proxy remains mutable and is intended for actions; reading it directly during render does not subscribe the component. Configure the compiler target for your React version; React 18 apps need the compiler runtime described in [React's target documentation](https://react.dev/reference/react-compiler/target).

Run `bun run test:react:compiler` for the installed-package matrix and `bun run test:browser` for compiled controlled inputs and memoized children in Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

## When to use each mode

| Mode | Best for | How it works |
|------|----------|--------------|
| `useClassyStore(store, selector)` | Derived values, primitives, specific slices | Selector runs on snapshot, compared with `Object.is` |
| `useClassyStore(store)` | Components reading many props, rapid prototyping | `proxy-compare` tracks reads automatically |
| `useClassyStore(store, selector, {isEqual: shallowEqual})` | Selectors returning new objects/arrays | Shallow comparison prevents unnecessary re-renders |
| `useClassyStore(store, selector)` | Controlled form fields | Always notifies React during the input event turn |

## Comparison with other libraries

| Feature | Classy Store | Zustand | MobX | Valtio |
|---------|-----------------|---------|------|--------|
| Class-based stores | Yes | No | Yes | No |
| No observer/Provider | Yes | Yes | No | Yes |
| Auto-tracking | Yes | No | Yes (observer) | Yes |
| Selector mode | Yes | Yes | No | Manual |
| Memoized computed | Yes (auto-memoized) | Manual | Yes (computed) | No |
| Immutable snapshots | Yes | No | No | Yes |
| Structural sharing | Yes | N/A | N/A | Yes |
| Built-in persistence | Yes (per-property transforms, versioning, cross-tab sync) | Yes (middleware) | No (separate pkg) | No (manual) |
| DevTools integration | Yes (`devtools()`) | Yes (middleware) | Yes (separate pkg) | Yes (`devtools()`) |
| Undo/Redo | Yes (`withHistory()`) | No (manual) | No (manual) | No (manual) |
| Bundle size | ~2.3 KB gzip | ~1.2KB | ~16KB | ~3KB |

## Vision

I wanted state management that feels like writing plain TypeScript.

- **A class is the store.** Define fields, methods, and getters — that's your state, your actions, and your derived values. The class *is* the type. TypeScript infers everything automatically.
- **Getters are computed values.** Write `get filtered()` and it's memoized with dependency tracking out of the box. It caches until a dependency changes.
- **Framework bindings that feel native.** React's `useClassyStore`, Vue's `useClassyStore` (ShallowRef), Svelte's `toSvelteStore`, Solid's `useClassyStore` (signal getter), Angular's `injectStore` — each integration matches the framework's reactive idioms.
- **Call methods directly.** `todoStore.addTodo('Buy milk')` — a real object with real methods, callable from anywhere.
- **Observe only what matters.** Components re-render when the specific properties they read change.

Clean, simple, and type-safe. That was the whole idea.

## Acknowledgements

This library wouldn't exist without the ideas pioneered by these projects. Each one taught us something different, and we took the best of each:

**[MobX](https://github.com/mobxjs/mobx)** — The OG of class-based reactive state. MobX proved that classes with fields, methods, and getters are the most natural way to model state. We took its `makeAutoObservable` philosophy — everything is reactive by default, no decorators or boilerplate — and its automatic computed memoization with fine-grained dependency tracking. MobX showed that getters should "just work" as cached derived values.

**[Valtio](https://github.com/pmndrs/valtio)** — Daishi Kato's proxy-based masterpiece gave us the core architectural pattern: a mutable write proxy for ergonomic mutations paired with immutable snapshots for React integration. Valtio's structural sharing approach — where unchanged sub-trees keep the same frozen reference across snapshots — is what makes `Object.is` selectors efficient without custom equality. We also adopted its `proxy-compare` library for automatic property tracking in selectorless mode.

**[Zustand](https://github.com/pmndrs/zustand)** — Also by Daishi Kato, Zustand set the standard for minimal, hook-first state management. Its selector pattern (`useClassyStore(store, s => s.count)`) with `Object.is` equality is what we use in selector mode. Zustand proved that you don't need Providers, context wrappers, or HOCs — just a hook and a store. Its focus on tiny bundle size pushed us to keep things lean.

**[proxy-compare](https://github.com/dai-shi/proxy-compare)** — The ~1KB utility (also by Dai-shi) that powers our auto-tracked mode. It wraps frozen snapshot objects in a tracking proxy, recording which properties a component reads, then efficiently diffs only those properties between snapshots. This eliminates the need for manual selectors in most cases.

**[React](https://react.dev)** — React 18's `useSyncExternalStore` is the foundation of our hook layer. It provides tear-free concurrent-mode-safe integration with external stores, and it's the same API used by Zustand, Redux, and Valtio under the hood.

**[Claude 4.6 Opus](https://anthropic.com)** — Let's be real: this library was designed, architected, implemented, tested, and documented almost entirely by Claude 4.6 Opus (Anthropic) via [Cursor](https://cursor.com). From the three-layer proxy architecture to the memoized computed getters with dependency tracking, the cross-snapshot caching strategy, and tests — it was all pair-programmed with an AI that never gets tired of writing Proxy traps. The human brought the vision, the taste, and the "no, make it better" energy. Claude brought the code.

# Upgrading to 0.8.0

Version 0.8.0 adds observable history and persistence status and simplifies the public API. This pre-1.0 release includes breaking changes for consumers of 0.7.x.

## Required updates

| Previous usage | Use in 0.8.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `persistence.unsubscribe()` | `persistence.dispose()` |
| Import `prepareStoreForHydration` from `/react` | Import it from `@codebelt/classy-store/react/server`, on both server and client |
| Import `getVersion` from the root entry | Use `subscribe()` for notifications or compare `snapshot()` references |
| Assume explicit persistence calls always resolve | Handle rejected promises from `save()`, `clear()`, and `rehydrate()` |
| Transform a property's value as a union of all store properties | Match `serialize` and `deserialize` to the property selected by `key` |

## Dispose persistence handles

Update effect cleanups and other teardown calls:

```ts
// Before
return () => persistence.unsubscribe();

// After
return () => persistence.dispose();
```

Disposal is idempotent. It stops subscriptions and timers, ignores pending read results, and cancels writes that have not started. Already-issued storage I/O cannot be cancelled. Explicit queued operations cancelled by disposal reject, as do explicit operations called after disposal.

## Handle explicit persistence failures

`save()`, `clear()`, and `rehydrate()` take no options. They report storage failures through `onError` and `lastError`, and reject their promises. Handle the promise even when an `onError` callback is configured:

```ts
try {
  await persistence.save();
  showSavedMessage();
} catch (error) {
  showSaveError(error);
}
```

Automatic writes and initial hydration handle reported failures internally. `hydrated` resolves when the initial attempt settles; `isHydrated` also means an attempt settled, including failure or a superseded read. Check `persistence.getSnapshot().lastError` when the result matters. A failed operation does not prevent later queued writes from running.

## Subscribe to utility status in React

Use `useClassyStore(store)` for store data. Use the new hooks when rendering utility metadata that can change independently of that data:

```tsx
import {useHistoryStatus, usePersistStatus} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

const {canUndo, canRedo, isPaused} = useHistoryStatus(history);
const {isHydrated, isExpired, lastError} = usePersistStatus(persistence);
```

Call these hooks inside a component or custom hook, with stable handles. Both status snapshots include `isDisposed`. History pause state now stays consistent when undo/redo finishes.

Outside React, handles expose `getSnapshot()`, `getServerSnapshot()`, and `subscribe(listener)`. The function returned by `subscribe` removes that status listener; `dispose()` tears down the utility handle itself. The shared status source implementation is internal. Consumer types are `HistoryHandle`, `HistoryStatus`, `PersistHandle`, and `PersistStatus`, exported from `@codebelt/classy-store/utils`.

During SSR and hydration, status hooks use the handle's initial status snapshot. Construct server and client handles with matching initial status.

## Use the hydration entry on server and client

```ts
import {prepareStoreForHydration} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react/server';
```

The `/react` entry exports React hooks and `createStoreHook`. Hydration preparation is exported only from `/react/server`; its captured-snapshot behavior is unchanged.

## Match persistence transforms to their property

Transform serializers receive the selected property's readonly snapshot value. Deserializers receive `unknown` and must return that property's mutable value. Validate stored values before returning them. Transforms that mutate their snapshot input or return another property's type now fail TypeScript checks.

Persistence status flags are readonly, matching their runtime getters. `PersistOperation` is exported from the utilities entry for typed error handlers.

If upgrading from 0.6.x or earlier, also follow the [0.7.0 upgrade guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/UPGRADING_0_7) for React timing options and the native `WeakRef` requirement.

---
SOURCE: https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/UPGRADING_0_7
---

# Upgrading to 0.7.0

This is the historical 0.7.0 upgrade guide. For the current API, also read [Upgrading to 0.8.0](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/UPGRADING_0_8), which replaces persistence cleanup and removes duplicate exports.

Version 0.7.0 focuses on core and React correctness, including controlled inputs, React Compiler, SSR, Next.js App Router, memory retention, and persistence. It includes React API and runtime changes that consumers upgrading from 0.6.x should review.

## Remove React timing options

React hooks now always subscribe synchronously. This keeps controlled inputs and their caret positions aligned with store updates. Remove `sync: true` and `sync: false` from both direct and bound hooks.

Before, in 0.6.x:

```tsx
const state = useClassyStore(store, {sync: true});
const count = useClassyStore(store, (state) => state.count, {sync: true});

// useCounterStore was created with createStoreHook(store).
const boundState = useCounterStore({sync: true});
const boundCount = useCounterStore((state) => state.count, {sync: true});
```

After, in 0.7.0:

```tsx
const state = useClassyStore(store);
const count = useClassyStore(store, (state) => state.count);

const boundState = useCounterStore();
const boundCount = useCounterStore((state) => state.count);
```

Auto-tracked hooks no longer accept an options argument, even an empty `{}`. Remove imports and annotations using the removed `UseClassyStoreOptions` type. Selector hooks still accept `UseClassyStoreSelectorOptions<S>` with `isEqual`:

```tsx
// Before
const selection = useClassyStore(store, selectSummary, {
  sync: true,
  isEqual: shallowEqual,
});

// After
const selection = useClassyStore(store, selectSummary, {
  isEqual: shallowEqual,
});
```

The same change applies to selector options passed to a bound hook. Existing calls without React timing options continue to work.

Ordinary `subscribe(store, listener)` callbacks still batch in a microtask, and core subscriptions retain their `{sync: true}` option. React selectors can run after each individual mutation, even when React batches the resulting renders into one commit. Keep selectors pure and able to read intermediate state during a multi-property update; this release does not introduce atomic transactions.

## Check the auto-tracking runtime requirement

Auto-tracked React hooks (`useClassyStore(store)` and bound hooks without a selector) now require native `WeakRef` support from ES2021. Weak references let mounted consumers release obsolete snapshots and collection values.

Check that every browser or server runtime running auto-tracked hooks supports `WeakRef`. Transpiling JavaScript does not supply native weak-reference behavior. If your supported runtime lacks it, use explicit selectors or retain 0.6.x until you can raise that runtime requirement. Selector hooks do not require `WeakRef`.

React 18 and 19 remain covered by the package compatibility tests. React Compiler works with both selector and auto-tracked hooks; no compiler opt-out is required.

## Prepare server-rendered stores before live updates

Client-only apps do not need hydration preparation. For server-rendered apps where persistence or another update can run before every Suspense boundary hydrates, call `prepareStoreForHydration(store)` on server and client stores initialized from matching data, before rendering or starting persistence.

```ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {prepareStoreForHydration} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react/server';

const store = prepareStoreForHydration(
  createClassyStore(new ProfileStore(initialData)),
);
```

Create a separate store for each server request. The prepared snapshot is retained for that store's lifetime; use a new store for a new request or an intentional reset. See the [SSR guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SSR) and [typed context example](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SCOPING).

The published `@codebelt/classy-store/react` entry now carries `use client`. In Next.js Server Components or other server-only modules, import preparation from `@codebelt/classy-store/react/server`. Hooks and the existing preparation export remain available from `/react` inside client modules and ordinary SSR. Pass serializable initial data across the Server Component boundary and construct the store inside a Client Provider; do not pass the store proxy across that boundary. See the [Next.js App Router guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_NEXT).

## Review persistence ordering and cleanup

The stored JSON envelope has not changed, so upgrading the library alone does not require a persisted-data migration or a change to your application's persistence `version`.

- Saves and removals requested through one persistence handle execute in request order. Each save captures the state when it is requested.
- Rehydration waits for that handle's prior writes and ignores read results superseded by a newer read, save, clear, local edit, or accepted storage event.
- `clear()` cancels pending auto-saves and removes storage after writes already requested. It does not reset the live store; a later edit can save again.
- `unsubscribe()` stops listeners and timers, ignores pending reads, and skips queued operations that have not started. It cannot cancel I/O already issued to an adapter. If you need a final save, await `handle.save()` before unsubscribing while the application is still running.
- Real browser tab synchronization ignores outdated storage events and avoids echo writes. Ordering is per handle; separate handles writing the same async storage key still need application or adapter coordination.

See the [persistence guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/PERSIST_TUTORIAL) for adapter, debounce, and cross-tab behavior.

## Release notes

### React integration

- Synchronous React subscriptions fix controlled-input caret jumps without configuration; core subscriptions remain batched by default.
- Selector or equality-function changes refresh selections without requiring a store mutation. Concurrent and abandoned renders keep their tracking isolated.
- Auto-tracking preserves reads reused by React Compiler and memoized children. It can conservatively retain earlier reads until the relevant snapshot object's identity changes.
- `prepareStoreForHydration` and the `/react/server` entry support delayed and streamed hydration, including persistence updates before a boundary hydrates.
- Next.js App Router package boundaries, request isolation, navigation, refresh, and cleanup have production packed-package coverage with Compiler off and on.
- A typed context example covers independent and nested stores, keyed resets, and effect-owned persistence cleanup.

### Core, utilities, and performance

- Undo/redo and persistence restore mutable nested state while preserving reactive collection methods and recorded snapshots.
- Frozen snapshot backing copies are reused across auto-tracked consumers, reducing repeated work in large forms and lists.
- Detached child proxies, obsolete snapshot clones, and retired React selections can be released, including after collection replacement and array truncation.
- `Snapshot<T>` preserves callable signatures for typed methods, overloads, and generic functions under strict TypeScript.
- Persistence orders asynchronous operations and rejects stale reads and storage events, with regression coverage for overlapping operations and real two-tab React inputs.

Validation includes core/React tests, three-browser input tests, packed React 18/19 consumers, Compiler off/on, streaming hydration, Next.js, render-count budgets, and heap-snapshot checks. Persistence, history, DevTools, and reactive collections also have combined happy-path coverage and public TypeScript checks.

# Classy Store Tutorial

`Classy Store` is a reactive state library for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid, and Angular built on ES proxies. You define state as plain classes, wrap them with `createClassyStore()`, and read them with the binding for your framework. There are no Providers, no observers, no reducers, and no extra TypeScript interfaces to define your state shape — just classes and a hook. The library is ~3.5 KB gzipped, batches ordinary subscriptions while notifying React synchronously, and uses structural sharing for efficient change detection.

## Quick Start

**1. Define a class:**

```ts
// stores.ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

class Counter {
  count = 0;

  increment() {
    this.count++;
  }
}

export const counterStore = createClassyStore(new Counter());
```

**2. Use it in a component:**

```tsx
// Counter.tsx
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import {counterStore} from './stores';

export function Counter() {
  const count = useClassyStore(counterStore, (state) => state.count);
  return <button onClick={counterStore.increment}>Count: {count}</button>;
}
```

That's it. No Provider wrapping your app. The store is a module-level singleton — import it wherever you need it.

## Defining Stores

A store is any class instance wrapped with `createClassyStore()`. State lives as properties, mutations are plain assignments, and computed values are `get` accessors.

```ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

class TodoStore {
  items: { id: number; text: string; done: boolean }[] = [];
  filter: 'all' | 'active' | 'done' = 'all';

  get remaining() {
    return this.items.filter((item) => !item.done).length;
  }

  get filtered() {
    if (this.filter === 'active') return this.items.filter((item) => !item.done);
    if (this.filter === 'done') return this.items.filter((item) => item.done);
    return this.items;
  }

  add(text: string) {
    this.items.push({id: Date.now(), text, done: false});
  }

  toggle(id: number) {
    const item = this.items.find((todo) => todo.id === id);
    if (item) item.done = !item.done;
  }

  remove(id: number) {
    this.items = this.items.filter((todo) => todo.id !== id);
  }
}

export const todoStore = createClassyStore(new TodoStore());
```

Key points:

- Methods mutate state by assigning to `this`. The proxy intercepts every write.
- `get` accessors work as computed values — they run against the proxied state, so they're always up to date.
- Nested objects and arrays (like `items` and each item inside it) are automatically wrapped in child proxies. `item.done = true` triggers a notification just like a top-level write.

## Reading State in React

`useClassyStore` has two modes. Pick the right one and your components only re-render when they need to.

### Selector mode

```ts
const count = useClassyStore(counterStore, (state) => state.count);
```

The selector receives an immutable snapshot and returns the slice you need. The component re-renders only when the selected value changes (compared with `Object.is`).

> **When to use:** Default choice. Best for render performance because it's explicit about what the component depends on.

### Auto-tracked mode

```ts
const snap = useClassyStore(counterStore);
// just use snap.count, snap.name, etc. in your JSX
```

No selector — you get back a tracking proxy over the snapshot. The library records which properties your component reads during render and only re-renders when one of those properties changes.

> **When to use:** When you'd need 3+ selectors in one component, when prototyping, or when the shape of data you access is dynamic.

### Custom equality with `shallowEqual`

By default, `useClassyStore` compares the selector's return value with `Object.is`, which is a reference check. This works perfectly for primitives and for selecting existing properties directly — structural sharing means that if `todos` didn't change, the snapshot returns the **same frozen array reference**, so `Object.is` returns `true` and the component skips the re-render.

```ts
// ✅ No shallowEqual needed — structural sharing keeps the reference stable
const count = useClassyStore(todoStore, (state) => state.items.length);
const todos = useClassyStore(todoStore, (state) => state.items);
```

The problem shows up when your selector **derives a new value** — calling `.filter()`, `.map()`, or using object spread always allocates a new array or object, even when the underlying data hasn't changed. `Object.is` sees a different reference and triggers a re-render.

`shallowEqual` fixes this by comparing one level deep: for arrays it checks length + each element with `Object.is`, and for objects it checks key count + each value with `Object.is`. It only works on plain objects and arrays — not on `Map`, `Set`, or class instances.

Without `shallowEqual` — `.filter()` creates a new array every time the snapshot updates, even if the todo items haven't changed:

```ts
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

// ❌ New array reference every snapshot → unnecessary re-renders
const active = useClassyStore(todoStore, (state) => state.items.filter((item) => !item.done));
```

With `shallowEqual` — compares the array contents, not the reference:

```ts
import {shallowEqual} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

// ✅ Only re-renders when the filtered items actually change
const active = useClassyStore(
  todoStore,
  (state) => state.items.filter((item) => !item.done),
  {isEqual: shallowEqual},
);
```

**Getters do NOT need `shallowEqual`.** Class getters benefit from cross-snapshot memoization: the library tracks which `this` properties a getter reads and caches the result. On subsequent snapshots, if those properties are structurally the same (same reference via structural sharing), the cached result is returned. This means getter results are stable across snapshots -- `Object.is` works out of the box:

```ts
// ✅ No shallowEqual needed — cross-snapshot memoization keeps getter results stable
const filtered = useClassyStore(todoStore, (state) => state.filtered);

// ✅ Primitives from getters also work fine
const remaining = useClassyStore(todoStore, (state) => state.remaining);
```

`shallowEqual` is only needed when the **selector itself** derives a new value (via `.filter()`, `.map()`, object spread, etc.) — not when selecting a getter that does the derivation internally.

> **When to use:** When your selector (not a getter) derives a new object or array inline. You don't need it when selecting existing properties, primitives, or class getters — structural sharing, cross-snapshot memoization, and `Object.is` already handle those.

### Decision guide

- **Use selectors by default.** They're explicit and produce the fewest re-renders.
- **Use auto-tracked mode** when you'd need 3+ selectors in one component or when you're exploring the API.
- **Add `shallowEqual`** when your selector returns objects/arrays and you're seeing unnecessary re-renders.

### Controlled inputs

React subscriptions always notify synchronously. React sees a field's updated value during the input event, so typing in the middle of a controlled input preserves its caret. Selector, auto-tracked, and bound hooks all use the same timing without configuration:

```tsx
class ProfileFormStore {
  name = '';

  setName(value: string) {
    this.name = value;
  }
}

const profileFormStore = createClassyStore(new ProfileFormStore());

function NameInput() {
  const name = useClassyStore(profileFormStore, (state) => state.name);

  return (
    <input
      value={name}
      onChange={(event) => profileFormStore.setName(event.target.value)}
    />
  );
}
```

When upgrading, remove the React `sync` option and `UseClassyStoreOptions` imports. Keep `isEqual` options if you use custom selector equality. The low-level `subscribe()` API retains its existing batching and optional `sync` setting.

## Batching

Ordinary `subscribe()` callbacks batch notifications in a microtask. React subscriptions instead notify after each mutation. React batches the resulting renders within an event handler, so a method that updates several fields can commit their final state together. This is not a transaction: selectors and getters may run between writes.

```ts
class FormStore {
  name = '';
  email = '';
  submitted = false;
  count = 0;

  submit(name: string, email: string) {
    this.name = name;       // immediately notifies React
    this.email = email;     // immediately notifies React
    this.submitted = true;  // React batches renders in an event handler
  }

  incrementMany(n: number) {
    for (let i = 0; i < n; i++) {
      this.count++;         // each write notifies React
    }
  }
}
```

For ordinary subscribers, `incrementMany(100)` produces one notification. React may check its selected value on every write; use efficient selectors and avoid depending on an exact render count outside an event handler.

Mutations separated by `await` can commit separately, allowing loading and result states to appear — see [Async Patterns](#async-patterns) below.

## Snapshots

`snapshot()` creates a deeply-frozen, immutable copy of the store's current state.

```ts
import {snapshot} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {counterStore} from './stores';

const snap = snapshot(counterStore);
console.log(snap.count); // read-only
snap.count = 5;          // throws in strict mode
```

> **When to use:** Logging, debugging, serialization, passing state to non-React code (e.g., a canvas renderer, a Web Worker message). Inside React, `useClassyStore` calls `snapshot()` for you — you rarely need it directly.

Snapshots use structural sharing: unchanged sub-trees return the same frozen reference. If you only mutated `store.name`, then `snapshot(store).settings === previousSnapshot.settings`. This is why selectors on nested objects are efficient — if the sub-tree didn't change, `Object.is` returns `true` and the component skips the re-render.

## Subscribing Outside React

`subscribe()` registers a callback that fires once per batched mutation. It returns an unsubscribe function.

```ts
import {subscribe, snapshot} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {counterStore} from './stores';

const unsub = subscribe(counterStore, () => {
  const snap = snapshot(counterStore);
  localStorage.setItem('counter', JSON.stringify(snap.count));
});

// later: unsub();
```

> **When to use:** Analytics events, `localStorage` persistence, WebSocket bridges, or any side effect that should react to store changes but isn't a React component.

## Nested State & Structural Sharing

Deep objects and arrays are automatically reactive. You don't need to do anything special.

```ts
class DocStore {
  metadata = {title: 'Untitled', author: 'Anonymous'};
  sections = [
    {id: 1, heading: 'Intro', body: 'Hello'},
    {id: 2, heading: 'Methods', body: 'We used proxies.'},
  ];
}

const docStore = createClassyStore(new DocStore());

// Deep mutation — triggers a notification
docStore.metadata.title = 'My Document';

// Array element mutation — also triggers a notification
docStore.sections[0].body = 'Updated intro';
```

While modifying nested properties directly through the proxy works, the same best practice applies here: prefer store methods over inline mutations. When nested updates are scattered across components, it becomes difficult to trace how deeply nested state changes. Methods give you a single place to look.

Structural sharing means that when you mutate `metadata.title`, the snapshot for `sections` is reused from the previous snapshot (same reference). A component selecting `(state) => state.sections` won't re-render because its selected value hasn't changed.

## Collections

Native `Map` and `Set` aren't plain objects — the proxy can't intercept their internal methods. Use `reactiveMap()` and `reactiveSet()` instead.

```ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {reactiveMap} from '@codebelt/classy-store/collections';

class UserStore {
  users = reactiveMap<string, { name: string; role: string }>();

  get count() {
    return this.users.size;
  }

  addUser(id: string, name: string) {
    this.users.set(id, {name, role: 'viewer'});
  }

  removeUser(id: string) {
    this.users.delete(id);
  }
}

export const userStore = createClassyStore(new UserStore());
```

`ReactiveMap` and `ReactiveSet` mirror the native API (`get`, `set`, `has`, `delete`, `clear`, `forEach`, iteration) but are backed by plain arrays so the proxy can track mutations.

> **When to use:** Whenever you'd reach for `Map` or `Set` inside a store. You *can* use native `Map`/`Set`, but only the reference is reactive — mutations like `.set()` or `.add()` won't trigger updates. You'd have to replace the entire Map/Set (e.g., `this.users = new Map(this.users)`) to notify subscribers. `reactiveMap()` and `reactiveSet()` avoid that by making individual operations reactive.

## Class Inheritance

Subclasses work out of the box — no special API or configuration needed. Methods, getters, and properties from all inheritance levels are fully reactive.

```ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

class BaseStore {
  loading = false;
  error: string | null = null;

  get hasError() {
    return this.error !== null;
  }

  setLoading(value: boolean) {
    this.loading = value;
  }

  setError(message: string | null) {
    this.error = message;
  }
}

class UserStore extends BaseStore {
  users: { id: string; name: string }[] = [];

  get activeCount() {
    return this.users.length;
  }

  async fetchUsers() {
    this.setLoading(true);       // base method — reactive
    this.setError(null);
    try {
      const res = await fetch('/api/users');
      this.users = await res.json();
    } catch (error) {
      this.setError(error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Failed');
    } finally {
      this.setLoading(false);
    }
  }
}

export const userStore = createClassyStore(new UserStore());
```

How it works:

- **Methods** from any ancestor class are found via the prototype chain and bound to the proxy. `this.setLoading(true)` inside `fetchUsers` goes through the SET trap just like a method defined on `UserStore` itself.
- **Getters** from all levels are automatically memoized. If `UserStore` overrides a base getter, the most-derived version wins. Non-overridden base getters work as-is.
- **`super` calls** work correctly — `super.setLoading(true)` dispatches through the prototype chain with `this` still bound to the proxy, so mutations are reactive.
- **`snapshot()`** preserves the full prototype chain, so `snapshot(userStore) instanceof UserStore` and `instanceof BaseStore` are both `true`.

> **When to use:** When multiple stores share common state or behavior. Extract the shared parts into a base class and extend it. The store proxy handles the rest.

## Async Patterns

Async methods work naturally. React is notified as each field changes, and pending asynchronous work lets it commit the loading state before the result arrives.

```ts
class PostStore {
  posts: { id: number; title: string }[] = [];
  loading = false;
  error: string | null = null;

  async fetchPosts() {
    this.loading = true;   // notify React that loading started
    this.error = null;
    try {
      const res = await fetch('/api/posts');
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      this.posts = await res.json(); // notify React that data arrived
    } catch (error) {
      this.error = error instanceof Error ? error.message : 'Unknown error';
    } finally {
      this.loading = false; // notify React that loading ended
    }
  }
}
```

A component selecting `loading` can show a spinner while the request is pending and remove it when the request finishes. React controls the exact render scheduling.

## Local Stores

Where you create a store determines its scope. A module-level store is shared by importers; `useLocalStore` creates one instance per mounted component. For SSR, use request-scoped or provider-owned stores instead of a shared server singleton.

### Basic usage

`useLocalStore` creates a reactive store scoped to the component's lifetime. Each component instance gets its own isolated store. Unmounting releases React's reference. Garbage collection can reclaim the store once no other references remain.

```tsx
import {useLocalStore, useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

class CounterStore {
  count = 0;
  get doubled() { return this.count * 2; }
  increment() { this.count++; }
}

function Counter() {
  const store = useLocalStore(() => new CounterStore());
  const count = useClassyStore(store, (state) => state.count);

  return <button onClick={() => store.increment()}>Count: {count}</button>;
}
```

The factory initializes component state. Subsequent re-renders reuse the same store instance; keep the initializer pure because React StrictMode can invoke it more than once in development.

### Persisting a local store

`persist()` owns subscriptions, timers, and optional browser listeners. Create the handle in an effect and dispose it in that effect's cleanup, including during Strict Mode replay. `useLocalStore` does not dispose application effects for you.

```tsx
import {useEffect} from 'react';
import {useLocalStore, useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import {persist} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

class FormStore {
  name = '';
  email = '';
  setName(v: string) { this.name = v; }
  setEmail(v: string) { this.email = v; }
}

function EditProfile() {
  const store = useLocalStore(() => new FormStore());
  // Auto-tracked mode — this component reads both name and email (see Decision guide).
  const snap = useClassyStore(store);

  useEffect(() => {
    const handle = persist(store, { storage: localStorage, name: 'edit-profile-draft' });
    return () => handle.dispose();
  }, [store]);

  return (
    <form>
      <input value={snap.name} onChange={(e) => store.setName(e.target.value)} />
      <input value={snap.email} onChange={(e) => store.setEmail(e.target.value)} />
    </form>
  );
}
```

The effect cleanup stops persistence. The store can be collected once React and any other owners release it.

## Creating a Bound Hook with `createStoreHook`

When you have a module-level store, you typically also export a typed hook for it:

```ts
// Before — manual boilerplate for each store
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import type {Snapshot} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

export const catalogStore = createClassyStore(new CatalogPageStore());

export function useCatalogStore<S>(
  selector: (snap: Snapshot<CatalogPageStore>) => S,
): S {
  return useClassyStore(catalogStore, selector);
}
```

`createStoreHook` does this in one line:

```ts
// After — one-liner
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {createStoreHook} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';

export const catalogStore = createClassyStore(new CatalogPageStore());
export const useCatalogStore = createStoreHook(catalogStore);
```

The returned hook supports both selector and auto-tracked modes, plus custom `isEqual` — identical to `useClassyStore`, but with the store already bound:

```tsx
// Selector mode
const count = useCatalogStore((state) => state.count);

// Auto-tracked mode
const snap = useCatalogStore();

// Custom equality
const data = useCatalogStore(
  (state) => ({count: state.count, loading: state.loading}),
  {isEqual: shallowEqual},
);
```

`createStoreHook` validates its argument immediately — if you pass something that isn't a store proxy, it throws at module load time rather than on first render.

## Tips & Gotchas

### Mutate through methods, not from components

While you *can* write `counterStore.count = 5` directly from a component, you shouldn't. Centralizing mutations in store methods keeps your logic in one place and makes it easier to find, refactor, and test.

```ts
// ✅ Good — mutation logic lives in the store
counterStore.increment();

// ❌ Avoid — mutation scattered across components
counterStore.count++;
```

When every state change goes through a method, you can search for callers of that method to understand how your state changes. When state is set directly from dozens of components, tracking down bugs becomes much harder.

### Don't use arrow functions for methods

Arrow function properties (`handler = () => {}`) are own properties whose `this` is lexically bound to the raw class instance at construction time. `.bind()` cannot override an arrow function's `this`, so when the proxy's GET trap binds it to the proxy receiver, the bind is silently ignored. Mutations inside the arrow function bypass the SET trap entirely — no notifications, no reactivity.

```ts
class Store {
  count = 0;

  // ❌ Arrow function — `this` is the raw object, mutations are invisible
  increment = () => {
    this.count++; // bypasses the proxy SET trap
  };

  // ✅ Prototype method — `this` is bound to the proxy by the GET trap
  increment() {
    this.count++; // goes through the proxy SET trap → reactive
  }
}
```

### Don't destructure the store outside `useClassyStore`

Destructuring copies the primitive value at that moment and breaks the proxy connection.

```ts
// ❌ Breaks reactivity — `count` is just the number 0
const {count} = counterStore;

// ✅ Always access through the proxy
counterStore.count;
```

### Non-proxyable types

Native `Date`, `RegExp`, `Map`, and `Set` use internal slots that proxies can't intercept. For `Map` and `Set`, use `reactiveMap()` and `reactiveSet()`. For `Date`, store timestamps as numbers and construct `Date` objects in getters or at render time.

### Set-then-revert and loop updates

React checks subscriptions after each write. Setting a field and reverting it in one event can still schedule rendering, even though the final displayed value is unchanged. Neither selector mode nor auto-tracked mode promises to avoid this work.

Likewise, a loop with a thousand writes sends a thousand synchronous React notifications. React can batch their renders within an event handler, but selectors may still run on each mutation. Ordinary `subscribe()` callbacks receive one microtask notification for that loop. For large updates, calculate the final value first when intermediate writes serve no purpose.

### Auto-tracked references

Each render gets its own read set. This keeps a suspended or abandoned render from changing the committed component's dependencies, and allows conditional reads to start from current store state. A shared proxy cache preserves unchanged tracked references across parent re-renders. Raw `snapshot(store)` caching and structural sharing are unchanged.

### Snapshot caching

Calling `snapshot()` multiple times without intervening mutations returns the same frozen object — an O(1) cache hit. There's no cost to calling it liberally.

```ts
import {snapshot} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

const a = snapshot(counterStore);
const b = snapshot(counterStore);
a === b; // true — same cached object

counterStore.increment();

const c = snapshot(counterStore);
a === c; // false — new snapshot after mutation
```

## Persistence

`persist()` saves your store's state to `localStorage` (or any storage adapter) and restores it on page load. It's a standalone utility function — import it from `@codebelt/classy-store/utils`.

```ts
import {persist} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

const handle = persist(todoStore, {
  storage: localStorage,
  name: 'todo-store',
});

// State survives page refreshes.
// Getters and methods are automatically excluded.
// Opt into cross-tab sync with syncTabs: true when using localStorage.
```

The persist utility supports per-property transforms (for `Date`, `ReactiveMap`, etc.), debounced writes, schema versioning with migration, merge strategies, TTL expiration (`expireIn`), SSR-safe `skipHydration`, and cross-tab synchronization.

For the full walkthrough, see the **[Persist Tutorial](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/PERSIST_TUTORIAL)**.

---
SOURCE: https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/ARCHITECTURE
---

# Classy Store — Architecture

Internal design documentation for contributors and maintainers.

## Three-Layer Architecture

The library is organized into three distinct layers, each with a single responsibility:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
  subgraph userCode ["User Code"]
    ClassDef["class MyStore { fields, methods, getters }"]
  end

  subgraph layer1 ["Layer 1: Write Proxy (core.ts)"]
    storeFn["createClassyStore(instance)"]
    SetTrap["SET trap: forward write → bump version → notify subscribers"]
    GetTrap["GET trap: return value, bind methods, lazy-wrap nested objects, memoize getters"]
    DeleteTrap["DELETE trap: same as SET"]
    Batch["queueMicrotask: coalesce synchronous mutations → 1 notification"]
    SyncNotify["sync listeners: notify immediately per mutation"]
    DeepProxy["Lazy deep proxy: nested objects/arrays wrapped on first access"]
  end

  subgraph layer2 ["Layer 2: Snapshot (snapshot.ts)"]
    SnapshotFn["snapshot(proxy): immutable deep copy"]
    StructuralShare["Structural sharing: unchanged refs reused across snapshots"]
    Freeze["Object.freeze: enforces immutability"]
    VersionCache["Version-stamped cache: skip rebuild if version unchanged"]
    GetterEval["Getters: memoized per-snapshot + cross-snapshot caching"]
  end

  subgraph layer3 ["Layer 3: React Hook (useClassyStore.ts)"]
    UseStore["useClassyStore(store, selector?)"]
    UseLocalStore["useLocalStore(factory)"]
    USES["useSyncExternalStore"]
    ProxyCompare["proxy-compare: track which snapshot props selector reads"]
    IsChanged["isChanged(prev, next, affected): fine-grained diff"]
    SelectorMode["Selector mode: Object.is or custom isEqual"]
  end

  subgraph component ["React Component"]
    Render["Re-render ONLY when accessed snapshot props change"]
  end

  ClassDef --> storeFn
  storeFn --> SetTrap
  storeFn --> GetTrap
  storeFn --> DeleteTrap
  SetTrap --> SyncNotify
  SetTrap --> Batch
  Batch --> SnapshotFn
  GetTrap --> DeepProxy
  SnapshotFn --> StructuralShare
  StructuralShare --> Freeze
  Freeze --> VersionCache
  VersionCache --> GetterEval
  UseStore --> USES
  USES --> VersionCache
  VersionCache --> ProxyCompare
  ProxyCompare --> IsChanged
  IsChanged --> Render
  SelectorMode --> Render
```

## File Map

The library lives in `packages/classy-store`. Public entry points expose the API;
implementation files and types live with the feature that owns them.

```text
packages/classy-store/
├── src/
│   ├── index.ts                         # Core public entry; no React dependency
│   ├── types.ts                         # Public Snapshot<T> and SubscribeOptions
│   ├── core/
│   │   ├── core.ts                      # Write proxies, subscriptions, computed getters
│   │   ├── core.types.ts                # Internal dependency and store bookkeeping types
│   │   ├── core.computed.test.ts        # Write-proxy getter memoization
│   │   └── core.ownership.test.ts       # Child ownership and subscription cleanup
│   ├── snapshot/
│   │   ├── snapshot.ts                  # Immutable snapshots and structural sharing
│   │   └── snapshot.computed.test.ts    # Snapshot getter memoization
│   ├── collections/
│   │   ├── index.ts                     # Public collections entry
│   │   └── collections.ts               # ReactiveMap and ReactiveSet
│   ├── frameworks/
│   │   └── react/

│   │       ├── server.ts                # Server-safe prepareStoreForHydration entry
│   │       ├── hooks/
```
