SOURCE: https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SSR
---

# React server rendering and hydration

Create one store for each server request and reconstruct a client store from the same initial data. Pass the store through props or React context. A module-level store on the server shares mutable state across requests and can expose one user's data to another.

The [typed context example](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_SCOPING) provides a complete provider pattern with independent instances, nested scopes, keyed resets, and persistence cleanup.

Import hydration preparation from `@codebelt/classy-store/react/server` in server code and client modules. This entry does not import React hooks. The separate `@codebelt/classy-store/react` hooks entry is marked `use client`. The [Next.js App Router guide](https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/REACT_NEXT) explains where to construct stores and how to cross that boundary with initial data.

Call `prepareStoreForHydration(store)` after initializing the store with the data used to render the page, on both the server and client. It captures that initial snapshot before persistence or other live updates begin. All direct and bound hooks use the captured data during server rendering and client hydration, then read the current live store. React requires the initial server and client data to match; see [React's external-store SSR guidance](https://react.dev/reference/react/useSyncExternalStore#adding-support-for-server-rendering).

## Initialize from request data

Keep the serialized payload limited to the data the client needs. Reconstruct the class so its methods and getters remain available:

```ts
// profileStore.ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';
import {prepareStoreForHydration} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react/server';

export type ProfileData = {
  name: string;
  visits: number;
};

export class ProfileStore {
  name: string;
  visits: number;

  constructor(initialData: ProfileData) {
    this.name = initialData.name;
    this.visits = initialData.visits;
  }

  recordVisit() {
    this.visits++;
  }
}

export function createProfileStore(initialData: ProfileData) {
  return prepareStoreForHydration(
    createClassyStore(new ProfileStore(initialData)),
  );
}
```

```tsx
// Profile.tsx
import {useClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import type {ProfileStore} from './profileStore';

export function Profile({store}: {store: ProfileStore}) {
  const state = useClassyStore(store);
  return (
    <button type="button" onClick={() => store.recordVisit()}>
      {state.name}: {state.visits}
    </button>
  );
}
```

For each request, render `<Profile store={createProfileStore(initialData)} />`. Transfer `initialData` using the framework's serialization facility and initialize the browser store from that same payload before hydration. If implementing the HTML transport yourself, use safe JSON serialization for the embedding context; do not interpolate raw JSON into an executable script. Class instances, functions, and native collection types need an explicit data representation.

For a store owned by a component, `prepareStoreForHydration(useLocalStore(() => new ProfileStore(initialData)))` captures its initial state while keeping its identity stable across renders. Preparation is idempotent. Keep the factory pure: React Strict Mode can evaluate it more than once in development. Changes to `initialData` after mounting do not automatically reset the store or its captured snapshot.

## Restore persistence while other boundaries hydrate

Browser storage may contain values different from the server-rendered payload. Prepare the store before starting persistence, attach persistence in an effect, and dispose it when the component unmounts. The effect can restore storage even while a Suspense boundary is still waiting to hydrate:

```tsx
// PersistedProfile.tsx
import {useEffect} from 'react';
import {useLocalStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react';
import {prepareStoreForHydration} from '@codebelt/classy-store/react/server';
import {persist} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';
import {Profile} from './Profile';
import {type ProfileData, ProfileStore} from './profileStore';

export function PersistedProfile({initialData}: {initialData: ProfileData}) {
  const store = prepareStoreForHydration(
    useLocalStore(() => new ProfileStore(initialData)),
  );

  useEffect(() => {
    const persistence = persist(store, {
      name: 'profile',
      storage: localStorage,
      skipHydration: true,
    });
    void persistence.rehydrate().catch((error) => console.error('Could not restore persisted state', error));
    return () => persistence.dispose();
  }, [store]);

  return <Profile store={store} />;
}
```

For example, the server renders `Server:1`, persistence restores `Saved:8`, and a delayed boundary then hydrates. The boundary first reads `Server:1` from the captured snapshot, reuses the server DOM, and then updates to `Saved:8` from the live store. It does not need an earlier hook read to establish the initial data. This applies to completed server HTML with selective hydration and to streamed Suspense content.

## Snapshot lifetime and scope

- Capture after loading the initial request data, before rendering or starting persistence. Preparation cannot recover earlier data if the store has already changed.
- Repeated calls return the same mutable proxy and retain the first snapshot. The capture is kept for the store's lifetime because another boundary or root may hydrate later. Use a fresh store for a different request or initial payload.
- Prepare the exact proxy passed to `useClassyStore` or `createStoreHook`. If a hook subscribes directly to a nested proxy, prepare that proxy separately.
- Capture follows ordinary `snapshot()` semantics. Plain objects, arrays, and supported class state are immutable snapshots; opaque leaves such as native `Date`, `Map`, and `Set` retain their identity. Replace those fields instead of mutating their native objects in place.
- Selectors read captured data during hydration and live data afterward. Their caches are separate, while equal selected results preserve reference identity at the handoff.

Client-only apps need no preparation. `createRoot` reads current state even for a prepared store. Unprepared stores retain the existing behavior of reading current state for server rendering and hydration, so keep them unchanged until every consumer hydrates if you do not use preparation. Neither preparation nor hydration resets the live store; `snapshot(store)` continues to return current data.

React subscriptions notify synchronously by default, including after hydration. Ordinary `subscribe(store, listener)` callbacks remain batched. The React hooks do not have a `sync` option. A normal sequence of mutations in an event can be batched into one React commit, but selectors may run after each mutation; this is not a transaction API.

---
SOURCE: https://codebelt.github.io/classy-store/docs/SUBSCRIBE_KEY_TUTORIAL
---

# subscribeKey Tutorial

`subscribeKey()` subscribes to changes on a single property of a store proxy. It's the property-level equivalent of `subscribe()` — instead of firing on every store mutation, it only fires when the specific key you're watching actually changes.

## Getting Started

### 1. Create a store

```ts
import {createClassyStore} from '@codebelt/classy-store';

class SettingsStore {
  theme: 'light' | 'dark' = 'light';
  fontSize = 14;
  language = 'en';

  setTheme(theme: 'light' | 'dark') {
    this.theme = theme;
  }

  setFontSize(size: number) {
    this.fontSize = size;
  }
}

export const settingsStore = createClassyStore(new SettingsStore());
```

### 2. Watch a single key

```ts
import {subscribeKey} from '@codebelt/classy-store/utils';

const unsub = subscribeKey(settingsStore, 'theme', (value, previousValue) => {
  console.log(`Theme changed from "${previousValue}" to "${value}"`);
  document.documentElement.setAttribute('data-theme', value);
});
```

Now only `theme` changes trigger the callback. Mutations to `fontSize` or `language` are ignored entirely.

### 3. Unsubscribe when done

```ts
unsub();
```

## Signature

```ts
function subscribeKey<T extends object, K extends keyof T & keyof Snapshot<T>>(
  proxyStore: T,
  key: K,
  callback: (value: Snapshot<T>[K], previousValue: Snapshot<T>[K]) => void,
  options?: SubscribeOptions,
): () => void;
```

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `proxyStore` | `T` | A reactive proxy created by `createClassyStore()` |
| `key` | `keyof T` | The property to watch |
| `callback` | `(value, previousValue) => void` | Called when the watched property changes |
| `options` | `SubscribeOptions` | Optional `{sync: true}` for immediate notifications; otherwise batched |
| **Returns** | `() => void` | Unsubscribe function |

The callback is not called when you subscribe. It receives the current and previous snapshot values when the watched key changes. By default, several synchronous writes coalesce into one callback with the final value; passing `{sync: true}` as the fourth argument observes each change. Import `Snapshot` from the root entry and `SubscribeOptions` from the root or utilities entry.

## How It Works

Under the hood, `subscribeKey` wraps the existing `subscribe()` + `snapshot()` APIs:

1. Captures an initial snapshot and stores `snapshot[key]` as the previous value.
2. On each batched notification (or each mutation with `sync: true`), takes a new snapshot and compares `snapshot[key]` with the previous value via `Object.is()`.
3. If different, fires the callback with `(currentValue, previousValue)` and updates the stored previous value.

Because `snapshot()` uses structural sharing, unchanged sub-trees return the same reference. This makes the `Object.is()` comparison efficient — no deep equality checks are needed.

## Use Cases

### Reacting to auth state changes

```ts
class AuthStore {
  token: string | null = null;
  user: { name: string; role: string } | null = null;

  login(token: string, user: { name: string; role: string }) {
    this.token = token;
    this.user = user;
  }

  logout() {
    this.token = null;
    this.user = null;
  }
}

const authStore = createClassyStore(new AuthStore());

// Redirect on login/logout
subscribeKey(authStore, 'token', (token, previousToken) => {
  if (token && !previousToken) {
    router.push('/dashboard');
  } else if (!token && previousToken) {
    router.push('/login');
  }
});
```

### Syncing with external systems

```ts
class PlayerStore {
  volume = 0.8;
  track: string | null = null;
  playing = false;

  setVolume(v: number) {
    this.volume = v;
  }

  play(track: string) {
    this.track = track;
    this.playing = true;
  }
}

const playerStore = createClassyStore(new PlayerStore());

// Sync volume slider with the Web Audio API
subscribeKey(playerStore, 'volume', (volume) => {
  audioContext.gainNode.gain.value = volume;
});

// Update document title when track changes
subscribeKey(playerStore, 'track', (track) => {
  document.title = track ? `Playing: ${track}` : 'Music Player';
});
```

### Logging specific changes

```ts
class CartStore {
  items: { id: string; qty: number }[] = [];
  coupon: string | null = null;

  get total() {
    return this.items.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.qty, 0);
  }

  addItem(id: string) {
    this.items.push({ id, qty: 1 });
  }

  applyCoupon(code: string) {
    this.coupon = code;
  }
}

const cartStore = createClassyStore(new CartStore());

// Only log when coupon changes — not on every item add
subscribeKey(cartStore, 'coupon', (coupon, prev) => {
  analytics.track('coupon_changed', { from: prev, to: coupon });
});
```

## subscribeKey vs subscribe

| | `subscribe()` | `subscribeKey()` |
|---|---|---|
| Fires on | Any mutation in the store | Only when the watched key changes |
| Callback args | `()` (no arguments) | `(value, previousValue)` |
| Use case | General side effects | Property-specific reactions |
| Overhead | Minimal | One snapshot comparison per mutation |

Use `subscribe()` when you need to react to any change. Use `subscribeKey()` when you only care about one property and want to avoid running your callback unnecessarily.

## Multiple Keys

To watch multiple keys independently, call `subscribeKey` once per key:

```ts
const unsub1 = subscribeKey(store, 'theme', handleThemeChange);
const unsub2 = subscribeKey(store, 'language', handleLanguageChange);

// Clean up both
function dispose() {
  unsub1();
  unsub2();
}
```

Each subscription is independent — they don't interfere with each other.

## Quick Reference

| What you want | How to do it |
|---|---|
| Watch a single property | `subscribeKey(store, 'key', (val, prev) => { ... })` |
| Stop watching | `const unsub = subscribeKey(...); unsub()` |
| Watch multiple properties | Call `subscribeKey()` once per key |
| Get both old and new value | Callback receives `(value, previousValue)` |
